author: Rahul kp
title: Price Elasticity
simple_words: Elasticity tells us by what percent demand changes when price changes by 1 percent.

definitions.meaning: Responsiveness of quantity demanded of a good to a change in its own price, other factors remaining constant.
Elastic: |Ed| > 1, quantity changes proportionately more than price. Inelastic: |Ed| < 1, quantity changes proportionately less.

key_points: Ed is a pure number: it has no units, so it does not depend on ₹ or kg.
For a normal downward-sloping demand curve, Ed is negative; we usually read its ==absolute value==.
Necessities tend to be inelastic; luxuries and goods with many substitutes tend to be elastic.
!!Perfectly elastic = infinity (horizontal curve); perfectly inelastic = 0 (vertical curve).!!

formulas.name: Percentage method
formulas.legend: Ed = price elasticity of demand; quantity demanded is of the same good; sign is negative on a normal demand curve.

formulas.name: Change-in-values form
formulas.legend: Q = original quantity, P = original price, ΔQ = change in quantity, ΔP = change in price.

formulas.name: Total outlay link
formulas.rhs: Price up: outlay falls if |Ed|>1, rises if <1, same if =1
formulas.legend: Outlay = P × Q, which equals the seller's total revenue.

insight.punchline: Elastic: price and outlay move opposite!
insight.text: If |Ed| > 1, a price rise cuts total revenue; if |Ed| < 1, the same price rise increases total revenue.

memory_trick.explanation: Elastic buyers escape when price rises, so revenue falls. Inelastic buyers stay stuck, so revenue rises. Unitary buyers: revenue stays same.

steps: Find ΔQ and ΔP from the data
Use original Q and original P
Name it: elastic, unitary or inelastic
exam_tip: In MCQs, first compare |Ed| with 1, then match the revenue effect. Check whether the question gives a price rise or fall.

doubt.question: Why is a flat demand curve not simply 'more elastic' at every point?
doubt.answer: Only a horizontal line is perfectly elastic. For a straight-line demand curve, Ed changes from point to point, high at top and low at bottom.

mistakes.wrong: Elasticity is the same as the slope of the demand curve
mistakes.right: Slope is ΔP/ΔQ in absolute units; Ed uses percentage changes, so it is unit-free and changes along a straight line.

mistakes.wrong: Perfectly inelastic demand means Ed = infinity
mistakes.right: Perfectly inelastic means Ed = 0 (vertical curve); perfectly elastic means Ed = infinity (horizontal curve).

mistakes.wrong: If |Ed| < 1, a price rise reduces total revenue
mistakes.right: If |Ed| < 1 (inelastic), a price rise increases total revenue because quantity falls proportionately less.

mistakes.wrong: Using the new price and quantity in the denominator
mistakes.right: In the basic formula, use the original price P and original quantity Q unless the question asks for the arc method.

Checker 1: simple_words: 'by what percent demand changes' mixes up a change in demand with a change in quantity demanded. Correct version: 'Elasticity tells us by what percent the quantity demanded changes when the price changes by 1 percent.'

Checker 1: Doubt question vs answer: the question asks about a 'flat' curve, but the answer talks about a horizontal line and a straight-line curve without connecting them. Correct version: 'A flatter curve is more elastic than a steeper one only when compared at the same price-quantity point. Along any single straight-line demand curve, Ed varies from point to point: it is greater than 1 above the midpoint, equal to 1 at the midpoint and less than 1 below it. Only a perfectly horizontal line has Ed = infinity at every point.'
